vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to go up and down many times
at a regular, even speed, without sudden changes
to go up slowly over a period of time
to reach the highest point before going down
a short, sudden rise that quickly goes down again
to fall suddenly and by a lot
to rise by a very small amount
to reach the lowest point and stop falling

paras: For three years, a chart hung on the wall outside Dana Ruiz’s office at the city transport department. It showed the number of bike trips in the city, month by month, for ten years. Most people walked past it. “A chart on a wall is just a line,” she says. “Nobody stops for a line. People stop for a story.”

So when the mayor asked her to explain the numbers in five minutes, she did not start with the data. She started with the shape. From 2015 to 2019, trips climbed steadily, from about 40,000 a day to 65,000. Then, in April 2020, they plunged by almost 70 percent in two weeks. “That was the easy part,” she says. “Everybody remembers April 2020.”

The surprising part came next. Trips bottomed out in May and then rose sharply. By September they had peaked at 92,000 a day, the highest number in the city’s history. People who had never cycled before had bought bikes. After that, the line started to fluctuate: a spike every summer, a dip every winter, and a slow, quiet climb underneath.

Since 2022, the number has edged up by about two percent a year. “That is the line that matters,” Dana says. “Not the spike. A sharp rise makes the news. A steady rise changes a city.” The city has built sixty kilometers of new bike lanes since then, and her five-minute story is the reason the budget was approved.

Her advice to anybody who presents numbers is simple. “Say what happened, say how big it was, and say why it matters. It rose, by how much, and so what. If you can do that in three sentences, people will remember the chart.”
reading.source: A composite portrait of a city transport analyst, written for this lesson.

choices: To report the exact number of bike trips in the city for every month and every year from 2015 to today.
To show how one analyst turned a chart into a story that people remembered.
To argue that cities should build more bike lanes.

listenings.text: Most people present a chart the same way. They put it on the screen and they describe it from left to right. In January the number was this, in February it was that. By March, the room has stopped listening. Here is what I teach instead. Before you show the chart, say one sentence that tells the whole story. Something like: our costs have climbed steadily for three years, and this quarter they rose sharply. Now the audience knows what to look for. Then give them only three numbers: where it started, where it ended, and how big the change was. From four million to six million, an increase of fifty percent. That is enough. Nobody remembers the fifth number. And finish with why it matters. A chart without a so what is just decoration.

And now a look at coffee. Prices for arabica beans have had a remarkable year. In January they were trading at about two dollars a pound. By the end of March, after a long dry season in Brazil, they had climbed to almost three dollars. Then, in May, they plunged by twenty percent in a single week, when the rain finally came. Since June, prices have fluctuated between two dollars forty and two dollars seventy. Analysts expect them to edge up again before the end of the year, as demand from Asia continues to grow steadily. For coffee drinkers, the news is mixed. Your morning cup probably won't get cheaper, but the sharp spike of last spring is unlikely to return. That's the market report for this week.
